title: Configuration
description: Global options, provider options, and per-request overrides.
body: Configuration FlexQuery is configured at three levels, and every level has one job: the more general one supplies defaults, the more specific one overrides them. Understanding this layering — and the immutability rule that guards it — is the difference between predictable behavior and order-of-initialization bugs. Every Configure method throws InvalidOperationException when called after a query has already executed. This is deliberate: query execution reads configuration concurrently, and a mutable global config is a race condition. Always configure during startup. Global options FlexQueryCore.Configure runs once at startup, before any query: Property Type Default Description DefaultQuerySyntax QuerySyntax NativeDsl Syntax used when no per-request syntax is supplied. DefaultPageSize int 20 Page size when the client omits one. MaxPageSize int 1000 Maximum page size a client may request. IncludeTotalCount bool true Compute total counts by default. StrictFieldValidation bool true Throw on unauthorized field access. MaxFieldDepth int 5 Maximum nested field-path depth. Global type maps FlexQueryOptions.CreateMap registers application-level entity → DTO maps that every typed execution reuses: Per-query CreateMap registrations take precedence over global maps. See Typed DTO Projection /docs/guides/typed-dto-projection . Provider options EF Core FlexQueryEFCore.Setup no delegate only registers the EF Core-specific operator handlers, such as like . UseNoTracking defaults execution to no-tracking; each call can override it opt.UseNoTracking = false . Dapper Dapper needs a model — there is no DbContext to reflect over: The SQL dialect is auto-detected from the DbConnection at runtime. The model must cover every entity you query — see Dapper /docs/providers/dapper for the full mapping API. Per-request overrides Every execution method accepts an optional Action delegate that wins over global/provider values: Typical per-request settings: governance sets see Security /docs/security , paging limits, query syntax, field mappings, per-query type maps, and the diagnostics listener. Precedence rules | Setting | Global | Provider | Per request | |---|---|---|---| | Default query syntax | ✔ | — | ✔ overrides global | | Page size defaults / limits | ✔ | — | ✔ overrides global | | Field governance | ✔ baseline | — | ✔ merges/overrides | | No-tracking behavior | — | ✔ default | ✔ per call | | Dapper model / timeout | — | ✔ | — | | Type maps | ✔ registry | — | ✔ per-query wins | Common mistakes Calling Configure inside a controller or on first request throws the immutability error as soon as any earlier query ran. Configure in Program.cs / Startup only. The defaults are convenient, not restrictive. Real endpoints set AllowedFields , MaxPageSize , and AllowedIncludes per request — see the defense-in-depth checklist /docs/security defense-in-depth-checklist .

title: Execution Pipeline
description: How a FlexQuery.NET request flows from query string to executed query.
body: Execution Pipeline Every FlexQuery call — whether it started as a query string, a fluent build, or an adapter request — flows through the same five-stage pipeline. Knowing the stages, their order, and what each one guarantees is what lets you predict result ordering, interpret validation errors, and place custom logic at the right point. The stages 1. Parse The syntax selected for the request global default or per-request override determines which parser runs. All parsers produce the same canonical QueryOptions — the rest of the pipeline is syntax-agnostic. Parse failures throw QueryParseException with the parameter name, syntax, raw value, and parser position details. 2. Validate The rule pipeline checks the parsed options against the entity model and governance configuration. Validation runs before any expression is built, so a rejected request costs no database work. See Validation /docs/guides/validation . 3. Apply The builder composes LINQ expressions in a fixed order: 1. Filter WHERE — narrows rows first; everything downstream operates on fewer rows. 2. GroupBy / Aggregates / Having — grouping forms after filtering; HAVING prunes groups before ordering. 3. Sort ORDER BY — orders rows or groups . 4. Paging OFFSET/FETCH or keyset seek predicates — slices from the ordered set. 5. Projection SELECT — last, so only requested fields materialize. 6. Total count — computed on the filtered set, independent of paging and projection. Paging before sorting would produce arbitrary page contents; projecting before filtering would hide filterable columns. The pipeline encodes SQL semantics, which is why result ordering and page boundaries are stable. 4. Translate - EF Core : the composed expression tree hands off to EF's translation — everything becomes SQL, includes hydrate via split queries. - Dapper : FlexQuery generates the SQL itself — select list surface-aware, type-map rewritten , joins for includes, WHERE, GROUP BY/HAVING, ORDER BY, paging — and executes via Dapper. 5. Execute The provider executes; results materialize into QueryResult with paging metadata, optional aggregates, and the optional cursor token. Cancellation is observed across the async overloads see provider notes for scope . Events Each stage emits an event that any IFlexQueryExecutionListener can observe: | Event | Fired when | |---|---| | QueryParsedEvent | Parameters have been parsed into QueryOptions . | | QueryTranslatedEvent | The provider translated the query SQL is available . | | QueryExecutedEvent | The database command completed includes timing . | | QueryMaterializedEvent | Results materialized into the result shape. | Attaching a listener is a one-liner opt.Listener = ... , and FlexQueryDiagnosticsCollector accumulates all four into a report — see Diagnostics /docs/diagnostics . Where client code fits - Before parse — authentication, rate limiting. - Between parse and execute — governance via the configure delegate, tenant scoping by wrapping the IQueryable before FlexQuery sees it. - After execute — serialization result-shape enforcement , diagnostics, response shaping.

title: Query Options
description: The QueryOptions model — every option the pipeline understands.
body: Query Options QueryOptions namespace FlexQuery.NET.Models is the parsed form of a request — the single model every execution method consumes, regardless of where the request came from query string, fluent builder, or adapter . Understanding its properties means understanding everything the pipeline can do. How a request becomes options Three equivalent paths, one destination: Most endpoints skip explicit construction entirely — FlexQueryAsync parameters, ... converts internally. Constructing QueryOptions yourself matters when composing: adapter output, pre-built saved queries, or merging client input with server-side structure. Properties Property Type Description Filter FilterGroup? Filter expression tree — conditions, nested groups, logic operators. See Filtering . Sort List<SortNode> Ordered sort specs field, direction, optional aggregate . See Sorting . Select List<SelectNode>? Projection tree — fields, aliases, nested selections. See Projection . Includes List<string>? Navigation paths to include with all scalars. See Include . Expand List<IncludeNode>? Expansion trees with per-branch filter/sort/take. See Expand . ProjectionMode ProjectionMode Output shaping: Nested default , Flat , FlatMixed . GroupBy List<string>? Group key fields. Aggregates List<Aggregate> Aggregate specs typed AggregateFunction + field + alias . Having HavingNode? Condition tree over aggregate values. Distinct bool? Applies Distinct . Paging PagingOptions Page, PageSize clamped 1–1000 , Disabled flag. IncludeCount bool? Whether the total count is computed. The three request models | Model | Use when | Where | |---|---|---| | FlexQueryParameters | ASP.NET Core FromQuery binding of raw strings. | FlexQuery.NET.Models | | FlexQueryRequest | Strongly-typed request objects OpenAPI-documented bodies . | FlexQuery.NET.Models | | QueryOptions | Composed server-side, adapter output, saved queries. | FlexQuery.NET.Models | FlexQueryRequest and FlexQueryParameters both expose ToQueryOptions with an optional syntax override ; QueryOptionsParser.Parse handles raw dictionaries for minimal-API and adapter scenarios. Projection modes in detail | Mode | Behavior | |---|---| | Nested | Nested selections produce nested objects — the natural hierarchical shape. | | Flat | Nested collections flatten with SelectMany into a leaf-level rowset SQL-join semantics . | | FlatMixed | Root scalars and nested-collection fields share one output row. | Complete worked example Composing client input with server-side constraints: Common mistakes Options built in code flow through the same validation as parsed requests. Hand-built options with unknown fields still fail — by design. QueryOptions is consumed by the pipeline; mutate it before calling FlexQueryAsync , not concurrently with it.

title: Query Result
description: The QueryResult<T> shape returned by every execution method.
body: Query Result Every execution method returns QueryResult — a uniform envelope that pairs the page of data with the metadata clients need for pagination UIs, aggregate displays, and cursor-based navigation. Because the envelope is the same for EF Core and Dapper, dynamic and typed results, your response contract never changes when the query does. Properties Property Type Description Data IReadOnlyList<T> The page of results entities, projected objects, or DTOs . TotalCount int? Total matching rows — or groups, on grouped queries. Null when counting is disabled. ResultCount int? Rows in the current page. Page int Current 1-based page number. PageSize int Effective page size after clamping . TotalPages int Computed from total count and page size. HasNextPage bool A next page exists. HasPreviousPage bool A previous page exists. Aggregates Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, object>>? Raw per-group aggregate values grouped queries only . NextCursorToken string? Cursor for the next keyset page keyset mode only . ResultShape IReadOnlyList<SelectOutputField>? The effective output surface when an explicit select is present. Null-valued optional members e.g. aggregates on non-grouped queries are omitted from the serialized payload. Serialization example Clients can build complete pagination UIs from this envelope alone: page numbers totalPages , next/previous buttons hasNextPage / hasPreviousPage , and row counts totalCount . Result shape and serialization enforcement When an explicit select is present, ResultShape describes the effective output surface — each output field with its name and source path. Serialization enforces this surface when the shape converter is registered AddFlexQuerySecurity / AddFlexQueryJson : anything outside the selected surface is removed from the payload, and aliases are applied on the way out. Clients therefore never see fields the query did not ask for, even when the underlying materialized object carries more. Grouped queries For grouped queries, Data contains one entry per group group keys plus aggregate aliases , and Aggregates exposes the raw per-group dictionary keyed by group key: totalCount is the number of groups after having — see Grouping & Aggregates /docs/guides/grouping for the full semantics. Keyset pagination When keyset mode is active, NextCursorToken carries the opaque, versioned cursor for the next page. It is null when the result set is exhausted — the standard end-of-scroll signal: Pass it back as the cursor parameter — see Keyset Pagination /docs/guides/keyset-pagination . Complete worked example Shaping a stable public response from the envelope: Common mistakes With includeCount=false , TotalCount is null — clients using it for "N results" UIs must handle that. Only rely on it when counting is enabled. Aggregates is populated only for grouped queries. On plain queries it is null — guard before reading.

title: Query Syntax
description: The three query languages — DSL, FQL, and MiniOData — and how to select them.
body: Query Syntax FlexQuery accepts three query languages on the same endpoint. All three parse into the same internal QueryOptions model — which means every feature in this documentation filtering, expand, aggregates, paging works identically regardless of the syntax a client uses. The syntax is a client-facing choice, not a server-side fork. | Syntax | Enum value | Style | Extra package | |---|---|---|---| | Native DSL | QuerySyntax.NativeDsl | filter=Status:eq:Active | built-in | | FQL | QuerySyntax.Fql | filter=Status = 'Active' | FlexQuery.NET.Parsers.Fql | | MiniOData | QuerySyntax.MiniOData | $filter=Status eq 'Active' | FlexQuery.NET.Parsers.MiniOData | Choosing a syntax : DSL is compact and URL-friendly — the default. FQL reads like SQL and suits developer-facing tools. MiniOData eases migration from OData consumers. Selecting the syntax Globally Per request Registering parsers The DSL parser is built in. FQL and MiniOData live in separate packages and must be registered once at startup: Registration before any execution; requesting an unregistered syntax throws ParserNotRegisteredException . Parameter map Both languages use the same parameter keys; only the expression grammar differs. | Parameter | DSL example | FQL example | MiniOData | |---|---|---|---| | Filter | filter=Status:eq:Active | filter=Status = 'Active' | $filter=Status eq 'Active' | | Sort | sort=Name:asc,Age:desc | sort=Name ASC, Age DESC | $orderby=Name asc, Age desc | | Select | select=Id,Name,Orders.Total | select=Id,Name | $select=Id,Name | | Include | include=Orders | include=Orders | $expand=Orders | | GroupBy | groupBy=Status | groupBy=Status | — | | Aggregate | aggregate=sum:Total,count:Id | aggregate=sum:Total,count:Id | — | | Having | having=sum:Total:gt:100 | having=sum Total 100 | — | | Page / PageSize | page=1&pageSize=20 | same | same | | Distinct | distinct=true | same | same | | Mode | mode=Flat | same | same | | Cursor / keyset | useKeysetPagination=true&cursor=... | same | same | The MiniOData parser supports $filter , $orderby , $select , and $expand . Grouping, aggregates, and having are DSL/FQL features. DSL filter grammar - Logical keywords AND / OR combine conditions — symbolic forms && , || are not supported in v4. - Collection operators any , all , count target collection navigations: Orders:any:Total:gt:100 . - Values containing spaces or reserved keywords must be quoted: City:eq:'New York' . - Null-check operators take no value: DeletedAt:isnull . FQL filter grammar FQL is SQL-inspired: values are quoted strings, operators are words or symbols, and parentheses group expressions: Aggregate syntax Aggregates use the dedicated aggregate parameter with function:field pairs: - Functions: sum , count , avg or average , min , max . - Aliases are generated in PascalCase by default sum:Total → output field SumTotal ; explicit aliases use function:field:alias . - Aggregates combine with groupBy ; having references declared aggregates: having=sum:Total:gt:100 . FQL aggregate sort spelling uses function parentheses: sort=SUM Total DESC . Sort syntax Both direction spellings are accepted: Aggregate sorts use function:target:direction DSL or SUM Field DESC FQL — see Sorting /docs/guides/sorting . Complete worked example One endpoint, three syntaxes, same result: All three produce identical results. Common mistakes filter=Status = 'Active'&sort=Name:asc mixes FQL filter syntax with DSL sort syntax. The whole request parses with one syntax — use one language per request. A global DefaultQuerySyntax = QuerySyntax.Fql without Fql.Register throws ParserNotRegisteredException on first use.

title: Diagnostics & Observability
description: Execution listeners, collectors, reports, and SQL inspection.
body: Diagnostics & Observability Dynamic queries are hard to debug precisely because they are dynamic: the SQL that executed depends on the request. FlexQuery.NET.Diagnostics exposes the pipeline as a stream of events — parse, translate, execute, materialize — that you can log, collect into a report, or inspect per stage. When a query misbehaves, the answer is in the events, not in guesses. Execution events Implement IFlexQueryExecutionListener namespace FlexQuery.NET.Execution to observe the four pipeline stages: | Event | Contains | |---|---| | QueryParsedEvent | Parsed QueryOptions snapshot — what the client actually asked for. | | QueryTranslatedEvent | Provider translation output e.g. the generated SQL . | | QueryExecutedEvent | Execution timing and outcome. | | QueryMaterializedEvent | Materialization details result shape . | Attach a listener per request through the execution options: Built-in listeners - ConsoleExecutionListener — writes each stage to the console; ideal for development. - FlexQueryDiagnosticsCollector — accumulates all events in memory for programmatic inspection. BuildReport aggregates the collected events into a FlexQueryDiagnosticsReport covering all four stages with durations — useful for request-scoped debug endpoints the sample application wraps this in a DiagnosticsHelper that attaches a __diagnostics object to responses during development . Attaching diagnostics to every production response leaks schema details. Gate them behind configuration, an admin role, or a query-string flag. SQL inspection Two provider-specific paths to the actual SQL: EF Core — ToSqlPreview ToSqlPreview uses EF Core's ToQueryString under the hood and works after dynamic projections are applied. ExplainProjection returns a human-readable plan: selected fields, navigation usage, and optimization notes. Dapper — SQL execution logging Every Dapper command logs an Information-level entry right before execution under logger category FlexQuery.NET.Dapper . The entry contains the final SQL formatted for readability, preceded by a DECLARE block embedding the parameter values — copy-paste-ready: The logging helper only reads the SQL and parameters already passed to Dapper — it never mutates or executes anything, and it short-circuits to a no-op when the logger is null or Information level is disabled. Complete worked example A timing endpoint for investigating a slow query: SQL formatter utilities The shared FlexQuery.NET.SqlFormatting namespace in the Diagnostics package exposes the SQL formatter used across providers — the same one that renders Dapper logs and translated SQL — for building custom tooling. Common mistakes A FlexQueryDiagnosticsCollector accumulates events — one instance per request, and Clear between uses. A shared instance mixes events from concurrent requests. When results look wrong, compare the parsed options stage 1 against the translated SQL stage 2 before suspecting execution — most surprises are translation-visible.

title: First Query
description: Build your first FlexQuery.NET endpoint with EF Core in a few minutes.
body: First Query This walkthrough builds a production-shaped ASP.NET Core endpoint that accepts dynamic query parameters and executes them against Entity Framework Core. It takes about five minutes, and everything you learn here composes with the rest of the documentation. What you are building One endpoint that handles, with no additional code: …as a server-side, validated, SQL-translated query — not in-memory LINQ. 0. Prerequisites - .NET 6, 8, or 10 project with EF Core set up and a Customer entity on a DbContext . - The packages installed: 1. Configure global options at startup Call FlexQueryCore.Configure once in Program.cs , before any query executes: These are defaults, not security — endpoints override them per request below. 2. Create the endpoint FlexQueryParameters is the model binder for query-string input. Pass it straight to FlexQueryAsync : What each line buys you: - AsNoTracking — read-only queries without change-tracking overhead. - AllowedFields — the only fields clients can filter, sort, or select on. - MaxPageSize — an endpoint-level ceiling clients cannot exceed it . - DefaultSortField — stable page boundaries even when clients omit sort . 3. Query it Response: What just happened 1. FlexQueryParameters bound the query string filter , sort , page , pageSize , select . 2. FlexQueryAsync parsed the parameters with the default syntax NativeDsl , validated every field against AllowedFields , and applied the pipeline — filter → sort → paging → projection — as SQL-translated expression trees. 3. Only selected columns left the database, and only allowed fields could be addressed. Variations Explicit query options When the query is composed server-side instead of parsed from the request: Typed DTO result Project into your own response type — same endpoint shape, documented contract: See Typed DTO Projection /docs/guides/typed-dto-projection for the mapping model CreateMap , ForMember , ForNavigation . Alternative query syntax Clients can address the same endpoint with FQL or MiniOData once the parser packages are installed and registered: See Query Syntax /docs/concepts/query-syntax . Next steps - Configuration /docs/concepts/configuration — the three configuration levels. - Filtering /docs/guides/filtering — the full operator reference. - Paging /docs/guides/paging — offset vs keyset modes. - Security & Governance /docs/security — locking endpoints down properly.

title: Expand
description: Deep, filtered, sorted navigation expansion trees.

headings.text: Filter, sort, and take per branch

body: Expand expand is include with control. Where include loads a whole related collection, expand lets each loaded branch carry its own filter, sort, and take — "give me every customer, but only their three most recent delivered orders". This is the pattern behind dashboard cards, order-history views, and any screen that shows a bounded slice of related data. Expand replaces the legacy FilteredIncludes API of v3. What expand does - Loads navigation properties like include , but each branch can specify: - filter — which related rows to load, - sort — their ordering, - take — how many to load. - Nesting composes: each child branch gets its own options. - Filters, sorts, and takes translate server-side — related rows are not loaded and then trimmed in memory. Grammar Basic expansion Filter, sort, and take per branch Options are semicolon-separated inside parentheses: The third example is the canonical dashboard query: every customer, each with their three most recent delivered orders. Deep and nested expansion Dotted paths and nested blocks express the same tree; nested blocks give per-child control: In the second form, Orders hydrates with two children — filtered items and sorted reviews — independently. FQL expand The FQL parser accepts the same structure with FQL expressions inside the options: Quoted values may contain semicolons and commas — tokenization happens before option splitting. Validation rules Expand is validated branch by branch, like the root query: - Each navigation path may be expanded at most once per query — merging duplicates would make filter/take/sort ambiguous, so duplicates are rejected. - Paths must be navigation properties that exist on the entity. - Branch filters and sorts obey the same field-existence, operator-validity, and type-compatibility rules as root filters. - An expand block with parentheses must contain at least one option — empty option lists are rejected. - All paths must be covered by AllowedIncludes when that governance set is configured. - Include and expand usage must stay consistent — the same path listed in include and separately expanded is a consistency error. Complete worked example A customer-overview endpoint with bounded, filtered graphs: Request: Response shape : The customer count and total are unaffected by the branch filter — the root query is independent of what gets expanded. Provider behavior - EF Core : branches hydrate via split queries; per-branch filter/sort/take translate into the split-query SQL, so a take=3 branch loads exactly three rows per parent. - Dapper : branches generate joins/subqueries; include-only joins are excluded from the count query; expand-block filter/sort fields are rewritten through nested type maps in typed DTO scenarios. Common mistakes expand=Orders filter=Status:eq:Delivered ,Orders take=3 fails. Merge into one branch: expand=Orders filter=Status:eq:Delivered; take=3 . Clients sometimes expect "customers with delivered orders" from expand=Orders filter=Status:eq:Delivered . It loads delivered orders per customer — customers without any still appear, with an empty array. To filter the root, use a root filter filter=Orders:any:Status:eq:Delivered . expand=Orders is rejected — either expand without options expand=Orders or provide at least one option.

title: Filtering
description: Filter operators, value formats, logical combination, and collection filters.
body: Filtering Filtering is the mechanism that turns a fixed "give me everything" endpoint into a flexible one: the client describes which rows it wants, and FlexQuery translates that description into a WHERE clause executed entirely by the database. Why it exists Without a query engine, every filter combination becomes a hand-written branch: This scales badly — ten optional filters produce a combinatorial explosion of overloads, each a potential SQL injection or translation bug. FlexQuery collapses all of it into one parameterized pipeline: the client sends filter=... , the engine parses it into a filter tree, validates every field and operator against your governance rules, and composes a safe expression tree that EF Core or the Dapper SQL builder translates to parameterized SQL. Client input never becomes raw SQL. Values are bound as parameters and fields are resolved against real CLR properties — an unknown field name fails validation before any expression is built. Filter grammar The native DSL expresses a condition as three colon-separated parts: Conditions combine with the AND and OR keywords no symbolic && / || in v4 , and parentheses group sub-expressions: FQL uses a SQL-inspired form instead — values are quoted, operators are words or symbols: Both languages parse into the same FilterGroup tree, so everything below applies to whichever syntax your clients use. Operators Comparison Operator DSL example FQL example Meaning eq Status:eq:Active Status = 'Active' Equality neq Status:neq:Active Status = 'Active' Inequality gt Total:gt:100 Total > 100 Greater than gte Total:gte:100 Total >= 100 Greater than or equal lt Total:lt:500 Total < 500 Less than lte Total:lte:500 Total <= 500 Less than or equal String matching Operator DSL example Meaning contains Name:contains:ana Substring search startswith Name:startswith:A Prefix match endswith Name:endswith:son Suffix match like Name:like:%ana% SQL LIKE pattern EF Core-specific handler Null checks Null-check operators take no value: Set membership and ranges Collection operators Collection operators apply a nested condition to the elements of a collection navigation — the SQL equivalent of EXISTS subqueries: The part before the operator names the collection navigation; everything after it is an ordinary condition evaluated per element. Common spellings map to the canonical operators — = , == , and equals all become eq ; > becomes gt ; sw becomes startswith ; cn becomes contains . Client ergonomics are free; your governance config only ever sees the canonical names. Value formats Values are parsed according to the field's CLR type: - Unquoted tokens work for identifiers, numbers, and booleans: Age:gte:18 , IsActive:eq:true . - Quoted strings are required when the value contains spaces or could collide with reserved keywords: City:eq:'New York' . - Dates use .NET-parseable formats: CreatedAt:gte:2026-01-01 . - Navigation paths are dot-separated and must point at scalar properties: Address.City:eq:Berlin . A quoted value inside FQL filters may contain commas and semicolons — the tokenizer handles quoting before option separators are split. Complete worked example A customer-search endpoint with role-checked fields: Request: Response: Generated SQL conceptually — EF Core translation : Every filter value is a parameter — the SQL text is fixed regardless of input. Configuration and governance | Option | Effect | |---|---| | AllowedFields / BlockedFields | Global allow/deny lists for any operation. | | FilterableFields | Restricts filtering to these fields only. | | AllowedOperators field | Per-field operator allow-list AllowOperators field, ... helper . | | MaxFieldDepth | Caps navigation-path depth e.g. Orders.Items.Price = depth 3 . | | StrictFieldValidation | When true default , violations throw QueryValidationException . | With the configuration above, filter=Salary:gt:100 and filter=Age:gt:18 operator not allowed both fail validation before touching the database. Rules and limitations - Field paths must resolve to real properties; typos are validation errors, not empty results. - like requires the EF Core provider; other providers should use contains / startswith / endswith . - Operators must be type-compatible with the field — Age:contains:25 fails the type-compatibility rule. - AND / OR are keywords; symbolic logical operators are rejected in v4. - Null-check operators take no value; supplying one is a parse error. Common mistakes filter=City:eq:New York fails because the value tokenizes into two parts. Quote it: filter=City:eq:'New York' . filter=Orders:gte:3 is not valid — a bare collection is not comparable. Use the count collection operator: filter=Orders:count:gte:3 . Without parentheses, conditions combine left-to-right in the order written. Group explicitly: A OR B AND C .

title: Fluent API
description: Build QueryOptions in code with the Query.Create fluent builders.
body: Fluent API Most FlexQuery requests arrive from clients as query strings and flow through FlexQueryParameters . But some queries are built by the server : composite endpoints, background jobs, internal reports, or anything where the "client" is your own code. The fluent API constructs the same QueryOptions the parsers produce — with compile-time structure instead of strings. Why use it - No string grammar — typos in filter=sum:Total:gt:100 are runtime parse errors; the fluent equivalent is checked as you write it. - Composable — builders compose from parts tenant scope + user sort + saved filter . - Same pipeline — the output is a regular QueryOptions ; validation, governance, and providers behave identically. Entry point Query.Create returns a FluentQueryBuilder . Every chain ends in Build — though the builder also converts implicitly to QueryOptions , so Build is optional at call sites that accept QueryOptions . Filter builder Filter takes a delegate over FilterBuilder . Conditions begin with a field selector and end with a value method: | Start | Purpose | |---|---| | Field name | Begin a condition. | | And name / Or name | Begin a condition with explicit logic. | | AndGroup ... / OrGroup ... | Begin a nested group. | | Not | Negates the next condition. | Condition terminators on FilterConditionBuilder : Each terminator returns control to the parent builder, so chains read linearly: This is equivalent to filter= Status:eq:Active AND Region:eq:EMEA OR Priority:gte:3 . Sort builder Aggregate sorts grouped queries use SortNode directly or the string-based sort on options. Select and include Expand Expand takes a delegate over ExpandBuilder . Each Path can carry a filter delegate over FilterGroupBuilder and nested children: This is the fluent equivalent of expand=Orders filter=Status:eq:Delivered ,Reviews Author . Grouping and aggregates Aggregate accepts Sum , Count , Avg , Min , Max ; an alias of null uses the default PascalCase alias SumTotal . Having function, field, operator, value builds a HavingConditionNode — it must reference a declared aggregate. Paging Complete worked example A server-composed "customer 360" query — tenant-scoped, filtered, with a bounded order graph: The built options flow through the exact same validation and execution pipeline as a parsed client request — governance still applies. You can mix both worlds: parse the client's query string for filter/sort, then compose additional server-side structure onto the resulting QueryOptions with the extension form options.Filter b => ... before executing. Common mistakes .Having ... references declared aggregates. Build .Aggregate ... first, or validation will reject the undeclared reference. .UseKeysetPagination 50 without any .Sort ... has no seek key. Add a deterministic sort ending in a unique column.

title: Grouping & Aggregates
description: GROUP BY, aggregate functions, HAVING, and grouped results.
body: Grouping & Aggregates Dashboards, reports, and summary bars all answer the same kind of question: how many , how much , what is the average — per category. SQL answers it with GROUP BY , aggregate functions, and HAVING . FlexQuery exposes the same trio through query parameters, so a client can pivot raw rows into summary rows without a bespoke endpoint per report. The three parameters | Parameter | Role | SQL equivalent | |---|---|---| | groupBy | Declares the group keys — the dimensions to summarize by. | GROUP BY | | aggregate | Declares computed values per group. | SUM x , COUNT , … in SELECT | | having | Filters groups by their computed values. | HAVING | A grouped query returns one row per group , not per entity — the result shape changes fundamentally, which is why grouping interacts differently with sorting, paging, and projection than plain queries do. GroupBy Multiple keys group by a combination: groupBy=Status,CustomerId produces one row per distinct Status, CustomerId pair. Aggregates Aggregates use a dedicated aggregate parameter with function:field pairs: Function Example Notes sum sum:Total Numeric fields. count count:Id Rows per group. avg or average avg:Age Numeric fields. min min:OrderDate Orderable fields. max max:OrderDate Orderable fields. Aliases Each aggregate produces an output field. By default the alias is PascalCase — sum:Total becomes SumTotal . Declare explicit aliases with a third segment: Rules: - Aliases must be valid identifiers and unique across the query. - Wildcard aggregates sum: are rejected. - Aggregates referenced by having or aggregate-sorts must be declared here — undeclared references fail validation. Having having filters groups not rows by computed values. It reuses the aggregate grammar for the left side and combines conditions with AND / OR and parentheses: Rules: - having without groupBy is a validation error — there is nothing to filter groups by. - Every aggregate referenced must be declared in aggregate . - Operators must be valid for the aggregate's result type. Pipeline order for grouped queries Grouped queries follow SQL semantics exactly: TotalCount on a grouped query is the number of groups after HAVING — paging metadata stays consistent with what the client sees. Complete worked example A revenue-by-status report with filtering and a HAVING floor: Request: Response: Data carries the projected group rows keys + aggregate aliases ; Aggregates exposes the raw per-group dictionary for clients that need machine-readable aggregate values. Governance - GroupableFields whitelists group keys. - AggregatableFields whitelists aggregate targets — critical, because aggregates like avg:Salary leak distribution data even when individual rows are blocked. - Sorting grouped queries is restricted to group keys and declared aggregates; unrelated sorts fail validation. Interaction with other features - Includes : grouped rows cannot carry arbitrary navigation collections — grouping plus unrelated includes is rejected. - Projection : select on a grouped query is constrained to keys and aggregate aliases the group-by projection rule . - Distinct : orthogonal — distinct=true deduplicates the ungrouped stream and is not combined with grouping. Common mistakes having=sum:Total:gt:100 without aggregate=sum:Total fails. The HAVING expression must reference aggregates that actually exist. aggregate=sum:Total alone does not produce a single grand-total row — aggregates are computed per group, and grouping is what defines the groups. Add groupBy even a constant-ish key to get summary rows. TotalCount is the group count on grouped queries. A client showing "137 orders" needs the ungrouped count — run that query without grouping.

title: Include
description: Load navigation properties with the include parameter.
body: Include Most APIs need related data — a customer and their orders, an order and its line items. Without includes, clients would need one request per level of the graph the N+1 request problem at the HTTP level . The include parameter loads navigation properties in the same request, hydrated by the database, not in memory. What include does - Loads the requested navigation s alongside the root rows. - Loads all scalar fields of each included navigation — include is "give me the whole related record". - Uses EF Core Include / ThenInclude translation or Dapper joins so hydration happens server-side. Response shape: Rules - Only navigation property paths are valid; scalar fields in the include list are rejected that is what select is for . - Dotted paths load nested levels: include=Orders.OrderItems loads each customer's orders and each order's items. - Unknown paths fail validation — includes can never silently load the wrong thing. - Duplicate include paths are rejected. Governance Includes expose data, so they are a governance surface: - AllowedIncludes or FieldAccess AllowedIncludes = ... whitelists which navigations clients may load. An empty set disables includes entirely. - Validation checks the whole path — AllowedIncludes = "Orders" permits include=Orders but rejects include=Orders.OrderItems unless Orders.OrderItems is also allowed wildcard patterns can express suffixes . Include vs expand | | include | expand | |---|---|---| | Purpose | Load a navigation with all scalars | Load a navigation with per-branch control | | Filter / sort / take | Not supported | Supported per branch | | Nested paths | Dotted paths | Nested blocks path child ... | | Governance | AllowedIncludes | AllowedIncludes | Use include when the client wants the entire related collection — it is the simplest and cheapest path. Use expand when the client needs only part of it: the last three orders, only delivered orders, a specific sort. Both are validated against AllowedIncludes . Complete worked example An order-detail endpoint that loads the customer and line items: Request: The include does not affect the filter or the total count — those apply to the root query. The result contains pending orders, each with its full orderItems array. Interaction with other features - select : selecting navigation fields select=Id,Orders.Total automatically derives the include tree — explicit include is only needed when the whole navigation should be loaded. - groupBy : grouping and unrelated includes conflict — validation rejects group-by queries that include navigations not covered by the group keys, because the grouped row shape cannot carry arbitrary collections. - Total count : includes never change totalCount ; counts are computed on the root entity set. Provider behavior - EF Core : includes translate to Include / ThenInclude ; hydration uses split queries so deep graphs stay efficient. - Dapper : include joins are generated for hydration and excluded from the count query to avoid join-multiplication inflating totals. Common mistakes include=Orders&select=Id,Orders.Total is redundant — the select tree already hydrates Orders . Redundant includes are not an error, but they load all scalar fields of Orders instead of only Total . An endpoint without AllowedIncludes lets clients traverse any navigation, including ones you did not intend to expose. Whitelist includes on every public endpoint.

title: Keyset Pagination
description: Cursor-based pagination for large datasets.
body: Keyset Pagination Offset pagination hides a scaling problem: OFFSET 100000 forces the database to walk and discard 100,000 rows before returning your 50. Page 10 is as cheap as page 1; page 10,000 is not. Keyset pagination also called seek or cursor pagination removes the offset entirely — instead of "skip N rows", the next query says "give me the rows after this one ", which turns page lookups into index seeks with constant cost. How it works 1. The client enables keyset mode and optionally sorts. 2. FlexQuery orders by the sort key and returns a page plus an opaque NextCursorToken describing the position after the last row. 3. The client sends that token back as cursor for the next page. 4. FlexQuery deserializes the cursor, validates it, and emits WHERE key, … last values… predicates instead of OFFSET . Reading the cursor The cursor rides on QueryResult .NextCursorToken : The token is versioned and serialized — clients treat it as opaque. On the next request it is deserialized and validated version check, value-shape check before use; a malformed or tampered cursor fails validation instead of producing wrong pages. Deterministic ordering is mandatory The cursor encodes the sorted column values. If two rows share the same key values, the seek boundary is ambiguous — rows can be skipped or returned twice across pages. sort=CreatedAt:desc,Id:desc is correct; sort=CreatedAt:desc alone can lose or duplicate rows that share a timestamp. If the client sends no sort, configure a DefaultSortField that ends in a unique column. Complete worked example An infinite-scroll feed: Client flow: Requirements and limitations - Forward only. There is no random page access — "go to page 57" is impossible by design. Clients that need page numbers use offset paging. - A sort or default sort is required — the cursor has nothing to seek on without one. - Mode conflict detection : sending both page and a cursor fails the pagination-mode validation rule. - Cursor values must be type-compatible with the sort columns. Choosing between offset and keyset | Scenario | Mode | |---|---| | Admin tables, page-number UIs | Offset | | Infinite scroll, feeds, mobile "load more" | Keyset | | Very large tables with deep navigation | Keyset | | Exports | Paging disabled | Low-level API: SeekAfter For hand-built queries outside the FlexQuery pipeline, the same mechanism is available as a LINQ extension on IOrderedQueryable : SeekAfter extracts the preceding OrderBy / ThenBy chain, requires at least one ordering throws InvalidOperationException otherwise , and generates the composite WHERE predicate for all of them — with Take n supplying the page size. Common mistakes Cursors encode positions , not page numbers. If rows are deleted between requests, a cursor still points at the same key — the next page continues correctly from there. But cursors are not bookmarks: do not persist them for "resume later" beyond a single navigation session. useKeysetPagination=true&page=3 is a conflict. Pick one mode per navigation flow.

title: Paging
description: Offset paging, clamping, disabling paging, total counts, and when to use keyset.

headings.text: Keyset vs offset: which mode when

body: Paging Paging controls how many rows a response contains. It exists to protect both sides: the database from unbounded scans, the client and your serialization layer from megabyte-scale payloads. FlexQuery ships two paging modes — offset paging by default and keyset cursor paging as an opt-in — and both compose with every other feature. Offset paging The client specifies a page number and size: Internally this becomes OFFSET 40 FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY or the dialect equivalent . page is 1-based; PagingOptions.Skip computes Page - 1 PageSize . Defaults and clamping All paging values are validated and clamped at usage time — a hostile or buggy client cannot force pageSize=1000000 or a negative page: | Input | Clamped to | |---|---| | page=0 or negative | 1 | | pageSize=0 or negative | 1 | | pageSize above limit | configured MaxPageSize default 1000 | Configure the limits globally and/or per request: Strict validation also guards the parameter shape : malformed page , pageSize , or distinct values fail with a parse error rather than silently defaulting. Total count and paging metadata When IncludeTotalCount is enabled default , FlexQuery runs a second, cheap query — COUNT over the filtered set, independent of paging — and the result carries full metadata: Clients use hasNextPage for "next" buttons and totalPages for page-number UIs. The count query costs a database round trip. Infinite-scroll clients never show totals — send includeCount=false or opt.IncludeTotalCount = false and FlexQuery skips the count query entirely. Disabling paging Some endpoints legitimately return everything — exports, small lookup tables, internal tools. Paging can be disabled in three ways: A paged-off endpoint with no row cap is a denial-of-service vector. Combine DisablePaging with upstream filters that bound the result set, or apply your own Take before FlexQuery sees the query. Complete worked example A customer list endpoint with paging governance: Requests and behavior: Keyset vs offset: which mode when | Scenario | Mode | Why | |---|---|---| | Admin tables with page-number navigation | Offset | Random page access needed. | | Infinite scroll / feeds | Keyset | Deep offset pages get slower linearly; keyset seeks. | | "Load more" mobile clients | Keyset | Forward-only navigation fits the cursor model. | | Exports | Paging disabled | Full result set with an upstream cap . | Deep-offset cost grows with page number: OFFSET 100000 still makes the database walk 100,000 rows. Keyset pagination replaces the offset with a WHERE predicate on the ordered key, so page 10,000 costs the same as page 1 — see Keyset Pagination /docs/guides/keyset-pagination . Interaction with other features - Grouping : for grouped queries, paging applies to groups after HAVING; TotalCount is the number of surviving groups, not raw rows. - Expand : include-only joins are excluded from the count query, so navigation hydration does not skew totals. - Keyset mode : offset parameters and an explicit cursor are mutually exclusive — the pagination-mode validation rejects the conflict. Common mistakes Without a sort or a configured DefaultSortField , database row order is arbitrary and pages can overlap. Always pair paging with a sort — ideally ending in a unique column. Never rely on client-side clamping. Set MaxPageSize per endpoint; the built-in 1000 ceiling is a backstop, not a design.

title: Projection
description: Field selection, aliases, nested selection, projection modes, and result shaping.
body: Projection Projection controls which fields the API returns. It is the quiet workhorse of API performance: selecting five columns instead of twenty-five reduces transferred bytes, serialization time, and — because the projection becomes part of the SQL SELECT — database I/O. Nothing unselected is ever materialized. Why it exists Entities are shaped for storage; responses are shaped for consumers. Returning whole entity graphs couples your database schema to every client and wastes bandwidth on fields the screen never shows. FlexQuery's select parameter lets the client pick the shape, while validation guarantees only allowed fields can leave the server. Flat selection Comma-separated field paths: Response rows contain exactly those fields JSON naming policy applies on the way out : Navigation paths Dot paths reach through navigations: Selecting a navigation path without loading the navigation fails validation with "navigation projection requires include". Add the path to include all scalars of the navigation or expand scoped, filtered loading . This rule exists because the projection must be backed by a loaded navigation to translate to SQL. Aliases Rename output fields — useful for DTO-style naming on entity-backed endpoints. Both spellings parse to the same output field: Both produce "firstName" or your configured naming policy sourced from the entity's CustomerFullName . Rules: - Aliases must be valid identifiers. - Exactly one alias per field — a:b:c is rejected. - Duplicate output names are rejected; alias conflicts are detected during tree merge. Nested selection Parentheses select a nested shape, and nesting composes arbitrarily deep: Nested and flat syntax mix freely: Nested selections imply loading — the referenced navigations hydrate as part of the query the include tree is derived from the selection tree . Projection modes mode controls how nested selections are shaped in the output: | Mode | Behavior | Use when | |---|---|---| | Nested default | Nested selections produce nested objects. | Hierarchical responses customer → orders . | | Flat | Nested collections flatten with SelectMany into a leaf-level rowset. | CSV-style exports, tabular grids. | | FlatMixed | Root scalars and nested-collection fields share one output row. | Denormalized report rows. | With Flat , one customer with three orders becomes three rows; FlatMixed yields three rows that each also carry the customer's scalar fields. Result shape enforcement When an explicit select is present, the response carries ResultShape — the effective output surface — and serialization enforces it: fields outside the surface are removed from the payload, using the selected aliases. Combined with AddFlexQuerySecurity / AddFlexQueryJson which registers the shape converter , the serialized JSON matches the requested surface exactly. Governance - SelectableFields or FieldAccess Selectable = ... whitelists selectable fields. - Field-depth limits MaxFieldDepth cap path nesting. - DTO surface protection rejects references to private or unmapped DTO members in typed scenarios see Typed DTO Projection /docs/guides/typed-dto-projection . Complete worked example A mobile endpoint that minimizes payload: Request and response: Interaction with other features - Aliases + Flat mode : aliases name the flattened output columns. - Grouping : grouped queries project group keys and aggregate aliases; select beyond that shape conflicts with the group-by projection rule. - Typed DTOs : select picks fields within the mapped DTO surface; the type map renames them see Typed DTO Projection /docs/guides/typed-dto-projection . Common mistakes select=Name:FullName,LastName:FullName fails — two fields map to one output name. Choose distinct aliases. Flat mode multiplies the root by the nested collection SQL-join semantics . If you want one row per customer, use Nested mode.

title: Sorting
description: Multi-column sorting, directions, default sorts, and aggregate sorts.

headings.text: How it works in the pipeline

body: Sorting Sorting determines the order of rows in a response. It looks trivial — until clients need "newest first, then by name", a default order for unsorted requests, and deterministic paging. FlexQuery handles all three in one pipeline stage that translates directly to ORDER BY on the database. Why it exists Client-driven sorting without a query engine means whitelisting sort keys by hand and string-building ORDER BY — a classic injection surface. FlexQuery parses the sort parameter into typed SortNode s, validates every field against SortableFields , and emits a parameter-safe ordering expression. The result is predictable, translatable ordering with no string concatenation. Syntax FlexQuery accepts two direction spellings, so both machine- and human-authored clients are comfortable: | Form | Example | Notes | |---|---|---| | Colon form | field:asc , field:desc | Native DSL canonical form. | | Space form | field asc , field desc | FQL-style; case-insensitive. | | Bare field | field | Defaults to ascending. | | Aggregate sort | sum:Total:desc DSL , SUM Total DESC FQL | Grouped queries only. | Multiple fields are comma-separated; the first field has the highest priority: How it works in the pipeline Sorting runs after filtering and grouping/having, and before paging. That ordering matters: 1. Filters narrow the rows. 2. Groups form if any and HAVING prunes them. 3. Sort orders the surviving rows/groups. 4. Paging slices a page from the sorted sequence. Because the sort is part of the translated SQL, ordering is stable across pages: an OFFSET page 2 continues exactly where page 1 ended. Sorting navigation properties Dot paths sort through navigations. The navigation must be loaded include or expand when it also appears in the response shape: For collection navigations, sorting by aggregate of the collection is a grouped-query feature — see below. Default sort When the client sends no sort , a configured default applies. This is important for two reasons: results are predictable, and databases return unspecified order arbitrarily — especially across pages. The FieldAccess attribute supports the same settings per endpoint: Governance - SortableFields or FieldAccess Sortable = ... whitelists sortable fields. Anything else fails validation in strict mode — this prevents clients from sorting by indexed but sensitive columns e.g. Ssn to probe data distribution. - Sorting grouped queries is restricted to group keys and declared aggregates see below . Aggregate sorts grouped queries In a grouped query, rows are groups — so sorting must reference either a group key or an aggregate value. Declare the aggregate, then sort by it: FQL aggregate-sort spelling uses function parentheses: Rules enforced by validation: - Every aggregate used in sort must reference a declared aggregate or at least be type-compatible with one . - count aggregates in sorts must target collection navigation properties — sorting by count:FirstName is rejected. - Sorting grouped results by fields that are neither group keys nor aggregates is rejected; the grouped shape has no meaningful per-row value for them. Complete worked example An orders dashboard sorted by revenue, with a deterministic tiebreaker: Request: Response: Keyset pagination and deterministic ordering Keyset pagination seeks using the sorted columns as the cursor. With a non-unique sort such as sort=CreatedAt:desc , rows sharing the same timestamp can be skipped or duplicated across pages. Always end the sort with a unique column: sort=CreatedAt:desc,Id:desc . Common mistakes Sorting works independently of select — sort=CreatedAt:desc orders correctly even if CreatedAt is not in the output. But the field must still exist and be sortable. If clients may omit sort , configure DefaultSortField — otherwise page boundaries are undefined and rows can repeat or vanish between pages.

title: Typed DTO Projection
description: Project entity graphs into your own DTOs with FlexQueryAsync<TEntity, TResponse>.
body: Typed DTO Projection The dynamic pipeline returns projected objects shaped at runtime. That is perfect for open-ended client-driven queries, but many endpoints have a known response contract — a CustomerDto your OpenAPI document promises, a CustomerSlimDto the mobile app consumes. FlexQueryAsync materializes results directly into your DTO types, with an AutoMapper-style mapping model that handles renamed members and renamed navigations. Why it exists Dynamic projection plus manual Adapt / Map code after execution has three problems: you lose server-side field selection the dynamic shape must include everything the map needs , serialization of anonymous shapes is hard to document, and mapping code scatters across controllers. The typed pipeline solves all three at once: 1. The query surface is computed from TResponse — only DTO-relevant columns are selected in SQL. 2. The projection is composed inside the EF Core expression tree or the Dapper SQL select list , so materialization lands directly in your DTO. 3. QueryResult is a strongly-typed, documentable result. QueryableEfCoreExtensions.FlexQueryAsync<TEntity, TResponse> and FlexQueryDapperExtensions.FlexQueryAsync<TEntity, TResponse> share the same mapping model. The mapping model Mapping follows AutoMapper conventions: - Convention : properties with the same name and compatible types map automatically. - ForMember dto = dto.X, entity = entity.Y : maps a renamed scalar — DTO member X is sourced from entity member Y . - ForNavigation dto = dto.Orders, entity = entity.Orders : maps a renamed navigation collection — DTO collection Orders is hydrated from entity navigation Orders even when their element types or names differ. Basic usage Properties that match by name Id , Email map by convention; Name maps when a type map or member expression supplies its source. Per-query maps The configure delegate registers a map for this call only: Global maps Application-wide maps are registered once at startup; per-query maps take precedence: How select interacts with DTOs The client's select controls which fields are queried and returned; the type map controls how fields are named on the DTO. Clients address DTO surface names — with a nested select tree, the response shape follows the requested surface: ResultShape on the response describes the effective output surface, and the registered result-shape JSON converter via AddFlexQuerySecurity or AddFlexQueryJson strips anything outside it — aliases included. Combining select and expand gives full control: the select tree shapes the response, expand controls which records load: Complete worked example A nested-select DTO endpoint from the sample application: With select=customerName,orders id,total , the response carries only the requested surface, renamed through the map, hydrated server-side in one query. Validation - DTO surface protection : only public, mapped surface members may be referenced by select/expand — private or unmapped DTO members are rejected. - Mapping expressions must reference public members on both source and destination types. - Client-addressed field names resolve through nested type maps: customerName in a filter or sort rewrites to the entity's CustomerName and onward to the physical column in Dapper SQL , so clients work in DTO vocabulary while the database works in entity vocabulary. Provider notes - EF Core : the projection composes into the EF expression tree; navigation graphs hydrate server-side; grouped queries materialize per-group rows through the grouped executor. - Dapper : SQL generation is surface-aware — projected property names are rewritten through the type map including JSON naming conventions , and include hydration merges nested DTO children after execution. Common mistakes select=someUnmappedField fails DTO surface protection. Add the mapping ForMember or extend the surface before clients can address it. A rename used by a single endpoint belongs in a per-query CreateMap . Global maps are for contracts reused across the application — otherwise the registry becomes a second source of truth to maintain.

title: Validation
description: How requests are validated, the rule pipeline, and error handling.
body: Validation Clients compose queries from untrusted input: field names that may not exist, operators that may not be supported, values that may not parse, and fields you never intended to expose. Validation is the layer that makes FlexQuery safe by default — every request is checked against your data model and governance rules after parsing and before any query executes , so invalid requests never reach the database. How validation fits the pipeline The separation matters: parse errors mean malformed syntax the client wrote something unintelligible , while validation errors mean well-formed but not allowed the field exists but is blocked, the operator is invalid for the type . Distinguishing them lets you return precise 400 responses and lets monitoring distinguish client bugs from probing. The rule pipeline Rules implement IValidationRule and each returns a ValidationResult : ValidationResult accumulates all errors Errors list, IsValid property , and ToErrorMessage formats them for humans: QueryValidationException carries the collected errors to your error handler. Rule families | Family | What it checks | |---|---| | Field existence | Filter, sort, select, having, and expand fields exist on the entity or the mapped surface . | | Operator validity | Filter/having operators are supported for the field type. | | Type compatibility | Values are compatible with field types — no contains on numbers, no string comparisons on dates. | | Field access | Fields respect AllowedFields / BlockedFields , per-operation sets, and the current role. | | Expand governance | Expand paths exist, are allowed, appear at most once, carry valid options, and stay consistent with includes. | | Aggregate rules | No wildcard aggregates; aggregates referenced by having/sort are declared; COUNT sort targets are collection-only. | | Having rules | Requires groupBy , valid operators, type-compatible values, existing fields. | | GroupBy rules | Projection, sort, and include conflicts for grouped queries. | | Projection rules | Select grammar, alias uniqueness, navigation projection requires include, DTO surface protection. | | Pagination rules | Offset/cursor mode conflicts, paging parameter validity. | | Governance config | The governance configuration itself is coherent unknown fields in allow-lists, etc. . | Strict vs non-strict mode StrictFieldValidation = true the default throws QueryValidationException immediately on unauthorized field access. In non-strict mode, field-access findings are recorded without aborting the pipeline — useful in staged rollouts, where you want to log what would be rejected before enforcing it. Exceptions | Exception | When | Useful members | |---|---|---| | FlexQueryException | Base of the hierarchy. | — | | QueryParseException | A parameter failed to parse. | ParameterName , syntax, raw value, parser Position / Expected / Found . | | QueryValidationException | Validation failed. | Collected validation errors. | | ParserNotRegisteredException | Requested syntax has no registered parser. | — | Complete worked example A hardened endpoint with full error handling: Example rejection: Design guidance - Fail loud in strict mode. Silent field dropping hides client bugs and governance drift; exceptions surface both. - Log rejected requests with their validation errors — they are your best signal for which surfaces clients actually want. - Pair validation with governance : validation checks what is possible does the field exist, is the operator valid ; governance checks what is permitted is it on the allow-list . Both run before execution.

title: AG Grid
description: Server-Side Row Model adapter for AG Grid.
body: AG Grid AG Grid's Server-Side Row Model SSRM sends a structured JSON request — paging window, filter model, sort model, row-group columns — and expects rows plus a row count back. FlexQuery.NET.Adapters.AgGrid translates that contract onto QueryOptions in one direction and the QueryResult back into the SSRM payload in the other, so a grid speaks directly to your database through the full FlexQuery pipeline. What the adapter maps | AG Grid concept | FlexQuery target | |---|---| | startRow / endRow | Paging window | | filterModel set, number, text, date, join operators | Filter conditions/groups | | sortModel | Sort nodes | | rowGroupCols + groupKeys | groupBy + group filters | | valueCols | Aggregates | Convert the request ToQueryOptions maps the entire request model; ToAgGridServerSideResponse produces the getRows payload rowData , rowCount , group metadata . Overloads exist for dynamic and typed results, and group rows serialize with their child keys so the grid can drill down. Applying onto existing options When you have endpoint defaults the grid should not override: Parsing raw JSON For minimal APIs or controllers that read the body as JsonElement : Complete worked example A row-grouped revenue grid — grouping and aggregates flow from the grid's column config: The grid's group drill-down sends the same request shape with groupKeys populated; the adapter turns those into group-key filters, and FlexQuery pages the matching rows. Adapter-produced options flow through the same validation pipeline. A grid column that is not in AllowedFields fails validation like any other request — whitelist grid-visible fields explicitly. Common mistakes SSRM expects the adapter's payload shape row count at the current level, group rows with child metadata . Always return via ToAgGridServerSideResponse , not the raw QueryResult .

title: ASP.NET Core
description: Controllers, [FieldAccess] security attributes, and JSON options.
body: ASP.NET Core FlexQuery.NET.AspNetCore binds FlexQuery to the MVC model-binding and filter pipeline. It adds three things: DI registration helpers, the FieldAccess attribute for per-endpoint governance, and the result-shape JSON converter that makes select surfaces authoritative in serialized output. Setup AddFlexQuerySecurity registers the FieldAccessFilter which reads FieldAccess attributes and the QueryResultShapeConverterFactory . AddFlexQueryJson registers only the JSON converter — for applications that manage security differently but want select-surface enforcement. A combined shortcut exists too: This performs FlexQueryCore.Configure configure global defaults and global type maps and returns the service collection. Endpoint pattern FieldAccessAttribute Apply on an action takes priority or the controller. All properties merge into the request's QueryExecutionOptions before validation: | Property | Purpose | |---|---| | Allowed | Allow-list of field names. | | Blocked | Blocked field names. | | Filterable | Fields clients may filter on. | | Sortable | Fields clients may sort by. | | Selectable | Fields clients may select. | | Groupable | Fields clients may group by. | | Aggregatable | Fields clients may aggregate. | | AllowedIncludes | Navigation paths clients may include or expand. | | DefaultSortField / DefaultSortDirection | Default ordering when the client does not sort. | | MaxDepth | Maximum nested field-path depth -1 = unset . | The filter resolves the attribute with action over controller priority, merges each list with any already-resolved execution options, and stores the result in HttpContext.Items for the execution methods to pick up. title: Overview
description: What FlexQuery.NET is, why it exists, and how the pieces fit together.
body: FlexQuery.NET Every dynamic API eventually reimplements the same query engine: optional filters that compose, sortable columns, paging metadata, field selection, related-data loading — each one hand-built, each one a potential injection surface. FlexQuery.NET is that engine, done once: it transforms query parameters sent by clients into secure, server-side expression trees that translate to SQL. GET /api/customers?filter=Status:eq:Active&sort=LastName:asc&page=1&pageSize=20&select=Id,FirstName,Email is handled by a single FlexQueryAsync call. Why FlexQuery.NET - No OData dependency — powerful querying without OData's complexity, setup, and tight coupling. - 100% server-side — all operations translate to SQL via expression trees. Nothing is fetched and filtered in memory; there is zero client evaluation. - Security first — declare allowed and blocked fields per endpoint; every request is validated against your model and governance rules before any query runs. - Multi-format — the native DSL, FQL SQL-inspired , and MiniOData syntaxes on the same endpoint, all parsing to one internal model. - Multiple providers — Entity Framework Core, Dapper, or any IQueryable source. - Observable — pipeline events, timing reports, and SQL previews built in. How it works 1. A client sends query parameters filter , sort , page , select , … or a JSON request model. 2. FlexQuery parses them into a QueryOptions model using the selected query syntax. 3. Validation checks every field and operator against your entity model and governance rules — rejected requests never reach the database. 4. The provider EF Core or Dapper applies the options as expressions or generated SQL. 5. A QueryResult returns data plus paging metadata, aggregates, and cursor tokens. The full pipeline is described in Execution Pipeline /docs/concepts/pipeline . Package ecosystem | Package | Purpose | |---|---| | FlexQuery.NET | Core query engine — parsing, filtering, sorting, paging, projection, validation | | FlexQuery.NET.EntityFrameworkCore | Async execution, includes, and typed DTO queries for EF Core | | FlexQuery.NET.Dapper | SQL generation and execution for Dapper | | FlexQuery.NET.AspNetCore | ASP.NET Core integration with FieldAccess security attributes | | FlexQuery.NET.Diagnostics | Execution diagnostics, timing, and observability | | FlexQuery.NET.OpenApi | OpenAPI/Swagger documentation for FlexQuery endpoints | | FlexQuery.NET.Adapters.AgGrid | AG Grid Server-Side Row Model request/response adapter | | FlexQuery.NET.Adapters.Kendo | Kendo UI DataSource request adapter | | FlexQuery.NET.Parsers.Fql | FQL FlexQuery Language syntax parser | | FlexQuery.NET.Parsers.MiniOData | Lightweight OData-compatible syntax parser | All packages target .NET 6, .NET 8, and .NET 10 FlexQuery.NET.OpenApi targets .NET 9 and .NET 10 . title: Dapper
description: FlexQuery for Dapper — model mapping, SQL generation, dialects, and logging.
body: Dapper FlexQuery.NET.Dapper generates and executes SQL directly against a DbConnection via Dapper — no ORM required. Because there is no DbContext to reflect over, the package asks you to declare a model: tables, keys, and relationships. From that model it builds complete SQL — select list, joins, WHERE, GROUP BY/HAVING, ORDER BY, paging — and hydrates results. Setup Configure the model once at startup: The SQL dialect identifier quoting, paging syntax is auto-detected from the connection at runtime — no manual dialect configuration. Entity<T> , ApplyConfiguration<T> IEntityTypeConfiguration<T> , and ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly assembly are supported — EF-style configuration classes work unchanged. Execution methods All methods live on FlexQueryDapperExtensions in namespace FlexQuery.NET.Dapper and extend DbConnection . Every overload accepts a CancellationToken . Dynamic results Typed DTO results Cancellation is observed while opening the connection, during diagnostics callbacks, and during materialization. Dapper's QueryAsync does not currently accept a token, so a running SQL command cannot be interrupted once started. SQL generation FlexQuery builds the full statement for you: - Select list — surface-aware: with a select , only those columns appear; in typed scenarios, property names are rewritten through the type map including JSON naming conventions . - Joins — generated for includes; include-only joins are excluded from the count query so join multiplication never inflates totals. - WHERE / GROUP BY / HAVING — the same semantics as the EF Core pipeline, expressed in dialect-correct SQL. - Paging — offset LIMIT/OFFSET or dialect equivalent or keyset seek predicates. - Expand — branches generate joins/subqueries with per-branch filter/sort/take. SQL logging When an ILogger is available, every Dapper command logs an Information-level entry right before execution under category FlexQuery.NET.Dapper . The entry contains the final SQL — formatted for readability — preceded by a DECLARE block embedding the parameter values, making it copy-paste-ready for query tools: Logging is strictly non-invasive: it only reads the SQL and parameters already passed to Dapper, and it is a no-op when the logger is null or Information is disabled. Complete worked example A minimal API endpoint over Dapper: Common mistakes The model must cover every queried entity and its included relationships — missing mappings surface as resolution errors at execution. Register all entities during Configure , or use ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly to sweep the whole assembly. Dialect auto-detection inspects the connection. Pass the actual connection of the target provider; a wrapper or mismatched connection produces wrong dialect SQL.

title: Entity Framework Core
description: FlexQueryAsync for EF Core — execution, includes, no-tracking, and SQL preview.
body: Entity Framework Core FlexQuery.NET.EntityFrameworkCore executes FlexQuery pipelines against IQueryable sources with full SQL translation. The package has one job: take the validated QueryOptions and compose them into EF Core expression trees — including split-query include hydration — so the database does all the work. Setup FlexQueryEFCore.Setup no delegate only registers the EF Core-specific operator handlers such as like . UseNoTracking defaults FlexQuery's execution to no-tracking; configuration becomes immutable after the first call. Execution methods All methods live on QueryableEfCoreExtensions in namespace FlexQuery.NET.EntityFrameworkCore . Every overload accepts a CancellationToken . Dynamic results Typed DTO results The two-type-generic overloads materialize directly into your DTOs: See Typed DTO Projection /docs/guides/typed-dto-projection for the full mapping model. No-tracking behavior FlexQuery defaults to no-tracking execution — results serialize without inverse-navigation fixup cycles, and read-only endpoints avoid the change-tracker cost. Override per call when you need tracked entities: With tracked queries, EF populates inverse navigations Order.Customer via relationship fixup. Configure ReferenceHandler.IgnoreCycles in the host JSON options so back-references serialize as null instead of throwing. The sample application demonstrates this with a tracked-query endpoint. Includes ApplyExpand translates the expand tree into EF Core Include / ThenInclude chains, each optionally filtered: Behavior details: - Include hydration uses split queries so deep graphs stay efficient. - Per-branch filters, sorts, and take values translate server-side — a take=3 branch loads exactly three rows per parent. - Navigation-projection selects select=Orders.Total also drive the include tree automatically; explicit ApplyExpand is only needed for standalone composition. Grouped queries groupBy / aggregate / having execute through the grouped-query executor: grouping and aggregates translate to SQL, HAVING prunes groups, and the executor materializes per-group rows with aggregate values into QueryResult.Aggregates . Paging on grouped queries pages groups after HAVING. SQL preview and projection explain Two inspection methods help during development and debugging: ToSqlPreview uses EF Core's ToQueryString under the hood and works after dynamic projections are applied. ExplainProjection returns a human-readable plan of selected fields, navigation usage, and optimization notes. Call ApplyExpand separately only when composing a queryable by hand before materializing yourself. body: Recipes Practical patterns assembled from the building blocks in the guides. Each recipe states the problem, the approach, and the working code. Cursor-driven infinite scroll Problem : a feed or list that clients scroll through indefinitely; offset pages get slower and rows shift between requests. Approach : keyset pagination with a deterministic sort unique trailing Id : The client appends cursor= to the next request. Deterministic ordering is mandatory — see Keyset Pagination /docs/guides/keyset-pagination . Role-based field visibility Problem : admins see more fields than support staff on the same endpoint. Approach : role-mapped field sets resolved from the principal: Requests outside the mapped roles fail validation — add a fallback role or map every role. Faceted dashboard with AG Grid Problem : an analytics grid where users group by a column and see sums/counts per group, with server-side paging. Approach : AG Grid SSRM's row-group/value columns map directly to grouping and aggregates — no custom code: Export endpoint no paging Problem : an export job needs the full result set. Approach : disable paging, skip the count query, and cap upstream: Combine DisablePaging with an upstream filter that bounds the set — an unpaged endpoint over an unbounded table is a denial-of-service vector. Search endpoint with contains + sort Problem : free-text search across name and email, ranked alphabetically. Approach : OR'd substring filters with a deterministic sort: For a LIKE -pattern search wildcards authored by the client , use the EF Core-specific like operator instead of contains . Per-tenant data isolation Problem : every query must be scoped to the caller's tenant, no matter what the client asks for. Approach : wrap the queryable before FlexQuery sees it — FlexQuery governs fields, you govern rows: Combine with RoleAllowedFields for column-level isolation. Public API with a strict surface Problem : a public read-only endpoint exposing exactly three fields, no includes, no deep paths. Approach : FieldAccess declares the whole contract on the controller: With AddFlexQuerySecurity registered, violations fail validation; the response surface is enforced at serialization too. Approach : typed DTO projection with a per-query map: Combine with a tight select to minimize payload size — see Typed DTO Projection /docs/guides/typed-dto-projection .
